improvement_notes: Clarify the sign convention for positive heading, positive angular velocity, and the coordinate frame before applying the proportional steering equation.

State explicitly that the breadth-first search is optimal only for the four-connected grid with equal movement cost; it is not a physically valid shortest-time or shortest-distance planner for a real rover.
Replace or qualify the phrase “current estimated motion” in the control definition, since the example primarily uses estimated pose and heading rather than velocity.

The lesson contains some repetition between the navigation-stack explanation, the text-equivalent diagram, the imagined hallway drawing, and the Python caveats. Consolidating these passages would improve pacing without reducing rigor.

Add one brief statement that a real differential-drive rover cannot execute an arbitrary grid displacement directly and must convert the desired motion into feasible curvature or wheel-speed commands.

The Python lab would teach more strongly if it printed a compact per-step state table containing estimated cell, target cell, and command, rather than repeatedly printing the entire map after every move.
The visual section says “Imagine a top-down drawing” immediately after presenting an actual visual. Reframe this as an interpretation exercise or remove the redundant drawing instructions.

The challenge mentions a safety limit but does not specify what the program should do if the limit is exceeded beyond stopping with a warning; require an explicit failure state and final verification guard.
Add a short accessibility note explaining that the diagrams’ signal flow and color-coded route elements are also described textually, and avoid relying on color alone in captions or instructions.

linkedin.title: Mobile Robot Navigation: From Localization and Planning to Physical Control
linkedin.description: A practical lesson on how mobile robots estimate pose, plan around obstacles, convert waypoints into motion, and expose the limits of simplified simulation.
linkedin.commentary:
A mobile robot does not simply receive a destination and drive there. It repeatedly estimates where it is, chooses where to go, and converts that decision into immediate motion.

This lesson introduces students to:
• The separation between localization, planning, and control
• The difference between a long-horizon route and an immediate motion command
• Distance, heading error, angle wrapping, and proportional steering
• A Python breadth-first-search simulation with obstacles and graceful no-route handling
• Real-world limits such as wheel slip, latency, robot size, and uncertain sensing

The lab is intentionally simplified, but it makes the navigation stack visible and gives students concrete experiments to run: change obstacles, block the goal, impose a move limit, or simulate failed motion.

Try the lab, then ask: what information would the rover need before it could safely trust its planned route?
